extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for authors writing historical-fiction stories or novels: how to research, build setting and characters, devise period-appropriate plot and conflict, and choose an approach (fictional characters in real events or biographical fiction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of historical fiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Historical fiction generally includes any story set more than fifty years in the past; it can include real people, fictional characters, or a combination, and may place characters within actual events or time periods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish historical fiction from contemporary fiction by timeframe (>50 years) and by the need for a more thorough historical approach. Treat people as products of their time; be intentional about where and when your story takes place.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research for historical authenticity
rubrics_metrics.description: Research is crucial to achieving historical accuracy and capturing the time and place of your story; great historical fiction brings specific periods and events to life so the reader feels they are experiencing the period alongside the characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gather information from primary and secondary sources (documents, newspapers, journals, books), and interview people who lived during the period or experts. Be thorough — e.g., Elizabeth Gilbert spent five years researching 1940s NYC, collecting details — but expect to use only a fraction of what you collect; research enriches context and provides material to infuse into scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build a vivid, period-accurate world
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct a historical world that feels authentic by answering concrete questions about daily life and the environment of the era.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate: Where did people live and shop? What was home life like? How did people travel and communicate? What work did men and women do? How were children educated? What entertainment, economy, clothing, slang existed? Use these specifics to evoke authenticity, but avoid overwhelming the narrative — include enough detail to create immersion while keeping focus on the story's core.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop characters shaped by historical context
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters must be formed by their historical circumstances rather than simply transposed modern people; create a detailed character study for protagonists that accounts for period influences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider culture, heritage, education, family, life events, socioeconomic status, and societal expectations when developing characters. Balance individual traits with period norms (example: Jo March in Little Women). For biographical fiction, research the person's life thoroughly; you may take creative liberties (e.g., imagined conversations), but keep portrayals grounded in facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Craft plot and conflict believable for the time period
rubrics_metrics.description: Plotlines and conflicts must be plausible within the historical context you’ve chosen — avoid plots that feel anachronistic or unlikely for that era.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check plausibility with period conditions (economic realities, technology, social norms). Use exercises such as imagining a scene or conflict across different time periods to see how responses change. Aim for a compelling plot and gripping conflict that readers will buy into by matching the right plot and conflict to the chosen time period (example: farm family during the Great Depression is believable; an inventor becoming an instant millionaire during the Depression may be less so).

rubrics_metrics.name: Approaches to starting historical fiction (two main methods)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two common ways to approach historical fiction: place fictional characters into real events/eras, or base the story on the life of a real person (biographical historical fiction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When placing fictional characters in real events, use the historical backdrop as the vessel for personal stories (examples: The Four Winds, The Bookwoman of Troublesome Creek, All the Light We Cannot See). When basing on real people, rely on deep research and fill gaps with plausible fictional scenes true to the person's life and personality (example: Z: A Novel of Zelda Fitzgerald). Be intentional about which approach suits your story and use research to inform whatever liberties you take.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance historical accuracy with narrative creativity
rubrics_metrics.description: Successful historical fiction balances fidelity to facts and period detail with imaginative storytelling — transporting readers to the past without letting history swamp the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid two anti-patterns: (1) slavish fidelity that turns the novel into a history lesson, and (2) careless anachronism or implausible liberties that break believability. Use research as a resource rather than a script; pick details that serve character and plot. Fill information gaps with plausible, character-driven inventions that respect the period’s realities.
